lines.text: Now the turning share. Alpha, a Greek letter like a little fish, is how fast the spin changes, in radians per second squared.
When the spin speeds up, a wheel a distance r from the center speeds up sideways by alpha times r.
Our wheels are ten inches forward and ten to the side. By Pythagoras, r is zero point three five nine meters.
With our turning cap of eight, that's two point eight seven meters per second squared.
Driving and spin-up push at right angles, so they add like a right triangle. The long side must stay under ten.
So driving still gets the square root of one hundred minus eight point two six: nine point five eight.
A hard spin-up costs only four percent of the drive.
Too big? The code finds one scale: ten over the long side. With ten and two point eight seven, that's zero point nine six one.
Both parts get the same scale. The triangle keeps its shape, so the robot keeps its direction.
In our simulator, about eighty percent of slip came from sudden spin steps. Lowering the turning limits cut it about six times, at no cost in time.
